newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Portugal, Indonesia begin East Timor talks at U.N.
newsitem.headline: Portugal, Indonesia begin East Timor talks at U.N.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday convened the first meeting in nearly a year between the foreign ministers of Indonesia and Portugal on the tricky question of East Timor.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said Annan opened the session, which was to be run by his special envoy Jamsheed Marker of Pakistan. The meeting, which was to end on Friday, will dwell mainly on procedure in hopes more talks can be scheduled for mid-July and the momentum can be kept going with subsequent sessions.
"I hope nobody expects we will go immediately into the substance. We have to lay the groundwork for the talks themselves," Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said.

Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its former colony. The territory was incorporated the following year as Indonesia's 27th province in an action not recognised by the international community.
Talks under U.N. auspices to find an internationally acceptable solution to the situation were initiated in 1983 by then Secretary-General Javier Perez de Cuellar.

The current meetings between Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama and Alatas will be the ninth in the series but the first under Annan, who took office in January. U.N. officials acknowledged the two sides were still far apart.
Gama said Portugal wanted "an improvement of human rights standards in order to get a comprehensive and internationally accepted solution to that problem."
Portugal insisted East Timor must be decolonized and its inhabitants allowed to determine their own future.
Indonesia argued that East Timor was decolonized as a result of a decision by its inhabitants to opt for independence through integration with Indonesia.

It denied charges by Portugal and others of large-scale human rights violations and said the Fretilin guerrillas who proclaimed East Timor's independence in 1975 as the territory erupted in civil war represented only a minority of the population.
Both Gama and Alatas said they felt Marker's role was positive in visiting their respective countries as well as East Timor.
Reiterating Indonesia's case, Alatas told Reuters on Wednesday that the Portuguese "left East Timor the same way (they) left Angola and Mozambique. So the East Timorese decolonized themselves."

But the Indonesian minister was not convinced the Portuguese were as committed to finding a solution,hoping instead for a change of government in Jakarta. He said any negotiations, by definition, involved a compromise.
